nameStory: The forget-me-not gets its romantic name from European folklore, where lovers would give these tiny blue flowers as tokens of remembrance. The 'early' part of this species' name refers to its habit of blooming earlier in the season than most other forget-me-nots, often appearing as soon as winter loosens its grip.
description: Early forget-me-not is a small, delicate annual plant that grows close to the ground in a low, spreading rosette. This tiny member of the borage family typically reaches only 2-6 inches tall, making it easy to overlook among other spring vegetation. Its most distinctive feature is clusters of miniature flowers that can be white, pale blue, or sometimes pink, each no bigger than a pencil eraser.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny five-petaled flowers, usually white or very pale blue, arranged in small curved clusters that unfurl like a scorpion's tail - which explains the alternate name 'scorpion grass'

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves covered in soft, fine hairs that give them a slightly fuzzy texture when you gently brush them with your finger

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats or rosettes that hug the ground, rarely growing taller than your hand is wide

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny, hard nutlets that are smooth and shiny, about the size of a pinhead

habitat: Look for early forget-me-not in sandy or gravelly soils in open, disturbed areas like roadsides, old fields, and woodland edges. It thrives in well-drained, often poor soils where many other plants struggle to establish. You'll often find it mixed with other small spring annuals in areas that get good sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear early, often in April and May, making this one of the first forget-me-nots you'll see blooming. Young plants form small rosettes of fuzzy leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants typically finish flowering by early summer and begin setting seed. The tiny nutlets ripen and the plants may die back in hot, dry weather.
seasonality.fall: Seeds germinate in fall, forming small overwintering rosettes that will bloom the following spring.
seasonality.winter: Small leaf rosettes may persist under snow cover, appearing as tiny patches of fuzzy green leaves in protected spots.

funFact: Despite being called 'early forget-me-not,' this little plant is actually one of the most forgettable members of its family - it's so tiny and inconspicuous that it's only been documented 8 times by naturalists across all of New England, making it rarer than finding a four-leaf clover!
confusionNotes: Early forget-me-not is easily confused with other small forget-me-nots, especially field forget-me-not. The key difference is timing - early forget-me-not blooms first and typically has smaller, whiter flowers, while field forget-me-not blooms later with slightly larger, bluer flowers. Remember: 'early and white' versus 'later and bright blue.'
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the romantic 'forget-me-not' name fool you into expecting showy garden flowers - wild forget-me-nots are much smaller and more subtle than their cultivated cousins. Many people walk right past them without noticing these ground-hugging miniatures.
compareHints: Among New England's forget-me-nots, early forget-me-not is the smallest and most easily overlooked. Water forget-me-not grows much larger in wet areas, while wood forget-me-not (often grown in gardens) has showier blue flowers. Early forget-me-not's white or very pale flowers and tiny stature help distinguish it from its more colorful relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water forget-me-not is distinguished from other forget-me-not species by its preference for wet habitats and its perennial, mat-forming growth habit.
Blue forget-me-not is the most rigid and unbranched of all New England forget-me-nots, with distinctly smaller flowers than its relatives.
Wood forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring drier woodland soils versus wet areas, and it has a more compact growth habit.
Field forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring dry, disturbed soil rather than wet areas, and having more pronounced patent hairs on its stems.
Unlike the common water forget-me-not which stays bright blue and grows in wet areas, changing forget-me-not prefers drier disturbed soil and shows its telltale color progression.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, bay forget-me-not stands out for having the smallest flowers and most relaxed growth habit.
